title: Recent advances in ultrasonic treatment: Challenges and field applications for controlling harmful algal blooms (HABs)
authors: Park J, Church J, Son Y, Kim K, Lee WH
scale: Literature review of lab, pilot and field studies
dose: Various frequencies, intensities and exposure times (reviewed)
result: Review concluding that field efficacy of ultrasound for HAB control 'is still debatable', with only a few full-scale field tests. The authors' own tests: a commercial LG Sonic e-tank reduced Microcystis 43% vs 5% in the control after 4.8 days in 50 L reservoir water, but both fell similarly after 11 days; sound pressure dropped 85.6% within 1 m in a lab tank and 91.3-95.8% within 1 m in Daechung reservoir.
env_effects: Authors describe ultrasound as leaving no chemical residues; toxin release from lysed cells is discussed as a concern.
key_details: Narrative review of mechanisms (cavitation, gas-vesicle collapse), influencing factors (frequency, intensity, duration, cell morphology), toxin removal, pilot studies and scale-up challenges (flow, turbidity, HRT, light, nutrient loading). It adds original case studies. In the lab test, two 50 L containers of Daecheung reservoir water were inoculated with Microcystis (~300,000 cells/mL) with one control and no replication, run July 7-21, 2016; ultrasound improved reduction by 30-55.2% over control between 4.8 and 7.8 days, and the difference was gone by day 11. Hydrophone surveys showed stable frequencies but steep pressure attenuation (e.g. 53.73 Pa at the device to 6.79 Pa at 0.5 m and ~0.3 Pa at 10 m in the reservoir). The authors recommend multiple devices for large reservoirs.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record omits the paper's own unreplicated experiments: a transient 30-55% Microcystis reduction vs control that vanished by day 11, and >85% sound-pressure attenuation within 1 m.

title: Beating the blues: Is there any music in fighting cyanobacteria with ultrasound?
organism: Anabaena sp., Cylindrospermopsis raciborskii, Microcystis aeruginosa, Scenedesmus obliquus, Daphnia magna
dose: Four commercial Flexidal AL-10 pond transducers (square waves at ~20, 28 and 44 kHz; acoustic power 0.7 +/- 0.2 W) in 800 mL cultures
duration: 5-19 days (Anabaena 19 d, Cylindrospermopsis 10 d, Microcystis 7 d, Scenedesmus/Daphnia 5 d)
result: Ultrasound did not kill Anabaena (biovolume growth rate cut from 0.28 to 0.02 /d, but filaments fragmented and chlorophyll kept rising) and had little effect on Cylindrospermopsis. Microcystis chlorophyll growth rate was actually higher under ultrasound (0.74 vs 0.59 /d), and all Daphnia died within 15 min of exposure.
env_effects: All Daphnia magna exposed to ultrasound died within 15 min (all controls survived), removing grazing control of Scenedesmus.
key_details: Lab jar experiments (1 L jars, 800 mL, 25 C, 14:10 light-dark) run in 2007, with four transducer jars vs four untreated controls (n=4; Scenedesmus/Daphnia in duplicates). Endpoints were chlorophyll-a, biovolume, particle counts, particle volume and PSII efficiency, with t-tests on growth rates. Anabaena filaments shrank from 331 to 28 um (56 to 7 cells per filament), so particle counts rose. Scenedesmus biomass was lowered only by Daphnia alone; with ultrasound plus Daphnia it matched controls because the Daphnia died. The authors conclude the tested commercial devices are not a solution for cyanobacterial blooms.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record says Microcystis growth was unchanged; its chlorophyll-based growth rate was significantly higher under ultrasound (0.74 vs 0.59 /d). The record also omits the 100% Daphnia mortality within 15 min.

title: Effects of Hydrogen Peroxide and Ultrasound on Biomass Reduction and Toxin Release in the Cyanobacterium, Microcystis aeruginosa
authors: Lürling M, Meng D, Faassen EJ
dose: Commercial Flexidal AL-05 and AL-10 transducers, ~20/28/44 kHz block waves, acoustic power ~0.63-0.68 W
result: Chlorophyll-a rose as strongly under ultrasound as in the control; particle counts rose 1.2x vs 2.3x in controls and PSII efficiency fell only slightly (0.56 to 0.52-0.53). Dissolved microcystin share after 5 d was 19% vs 5% in controls; authors conclude commercial transducers are ineffective.

title: Evaluation of several end-of-pipe measures proposed to control cyanobacteria
authors: Lürling M, Waajen G, de Senerpont Domis LN
scale: Critical review of end-of-pipe measures incl. ultrasound
result: Field evidence for ultrasound is weak: in a 365,000 m3 reservoir with 10 x 2 x 100 W (200 kHz) units, chl-a was 81 (+/-56) ug/L before vs 74 (+/-42) ug/L during treatment, and a 9,000 m3 pond study (630 W, 22 kHz) showed no difference by the end. Field intensities (~5.5e-9 to 7e-8 W/mL) are orders of magnitude below lab intensities, and commercial 20-200 kHz units cannot resonate 60-70 nm gas vesicles.
env_effects: Targets symptoms rather than nutrient enrichment.
key_details: Critical review (Lurling et al., Aquatic Ecology 2016) of effective microorganisms, golden algae, plant extracts, ultrasound and mixing of non-stratifying waters. For ultrasound it re-analyses published field studies (data digitized from figures) and applies resonance physics to gas vesicle sizes. Cites controlled lab tests where commercial transducers (20, 28, 44 kHz, 0.7 W) failed to control Anabaena, Cylindrospermopsis, Microcystis or Scenedesmus even in 800 mL. Concludes these end-of-pipe measures treat symptoms and none is a widely applicable solution.
fulltext_discrepancy: None; record lacked the specific field re-analysis numbers.

title: Ultrasonic frequency effects on the removal of Microcystis aeruginosa
authors: Zhang G, Zhang P, Wang B, Liu H
duration: minutes (sampling every 2 min; 90% removal took 100 min at 80 W and 328 min at 32 W, 80 kHz)
result: Removal (OD684) followed first-order kinetics; k rose from 0.007 to 0.023 /min as power went from 32 to 80 W at 80 kHz, and was 0.114 /min at 1320 kHz vs 0.0224 /min at 20 kHz. Reaching 90% removal needed 100 min at 80 W (0.134 kWh) vs 328 min at 32 W (0.175 kWh).
env_effects: No microcystin release at 32 W for 5 min and little at 15 min (safe below 48 W); at 80 kHz, 80 W, 5 min raised extracellular microcystins from 0.87 to 3.1 ug/L (MC-LR 0 to 2.11 ug/L).
key_details: Bench study with lab-cultured M. aeruginosa in BG11 (near 10^9 cells/L at 14 days), sonicated in two home-made multi-frequency cells. Removal was tracked as OD684 decrease, so it reflects cell removal/decolorization rather than verified kill. Exponential- and stationary-phase cells responded similarly. Higher frequencies (410-1320 kHz) worked much better than 20-150 kHz, explained by resonance with gas-vesicle size. The authors recommend low power for drinking-water use to avoid toxin release; no replication statistics were reported in the extracted text.
fulltext_discrepancy: effect_pct was null; the paper reports times to 90% removal (100 min at 80 W, 80 kHz). The microcystin rise was 0.87 to 3.1 ug/L total extracellular microcystins, not 3.11.

title: Neglected methane production and toxicity risk in low-frequency ultrasound for controlling harmful algal blooms
authors: Xu H, Tang Z, Liang Z, Chen H, Dai X
scale: Lab microcosm glass bottles (18.5 cm tall, 7.2 cm diameter; 200 mL lake sediment + 300 mL water), 27 bottles (3 treatments x 3 sampling batches x triplicate)
dose: 29.4 kHz at 0.059 W/mL for 15 min, applied once before incubation
result: Sonication cut M. aeruginosa from 6.19 x 10^8 to 4.12 x 10^8 cells/L (33.49%), but microcystin was 20.54 ug/L right after treatment (5.70-fold higher than unsonicated) and peaked at 41.18 ug/L on day 6. Cumulative CH4 by day 40 was 531.40 vs 371.67 umol/dm2 (1.43-fold).
env_effects: Sonicated treatments went anaerobic immediately (DO 0.07 mg/L, ORP -360.03 mV on day 0, DO <0.1 mg/L until day 20); DOC and microcystin significantly higher than unsonicated throughout (p < 0.05); CH4 flux peaked at 41.43 vs 32.06 umol/dm2/d on day 17; shift in methanogen community.
key_details: Lab microcosms with sediment and filtered water from a campus landscape lake (Tongji University) during a bloom. Three treatments: sediment + water control, unsonicated M. aeruginosa, and pre-sonicated M. aeruginosa, each in triplicate with destructive sampling, incubated 40 days at 25 C. The design simulates bloom collapse after one sonication rather than ongoing field treatment. Both algae treatments became anoxic, but the sonicated one did so from day 0 while the unsonicated one did so by day 9-12.
fulltext_discrepancy: The setting is a lab bottle microcosm (500 mL per bottle), not a mesocosm. The record omits the 5.70-fold higher microcystin right after sonication (20.54 ug/L) and the 41.18 ug/L peak.

title: Variation of efficiencies and limits of ultrasonication for practical algal bloom control in fields
authors: Park J, Son Y, Lee WH
organism: Natural Microcystis sp.-dominated (>99%) reservoir water (Chungju Dam), South Korea
scale: Field test at Baekje weir, Geum River; 100 L pilot batch reactor; 4 m3 algal raceway pond with circulation
dose: 36, 108 and 175 kHz at 300-650 W; pilot power density 0.0030-0.0065 W/mL; raceway 7.5 x 10^-5 to 1.63 x 10^-4 W/mL
duration: 10-20 min in pilot tests; 60 min circulation (30 min cumulative exposure) in raceway
result: In the 100 L pilot, 10 min of sonication cut Chl-a and Microcystis cells by about 80% at all frequencies, and 20 min gave 80-90% reduction out to 1.0 m; within 5 min, reduction fell from ~80% at 0.1 m to 15% (Chl-a) at 1.0 m. In the 4 m3 raceway, 108 kHz-450 W and 175 kHz-650 W gave >40% Chl-a and >60% cell reduction after 10 min, with efficiency falling after 60 min.
env_effects: Extracellular microcystin rose as Chl-a fell, more at 36 kHz and at higher power (650 vs 300 W at 175 kHz).
key_details: Staged tests with a customized ultrasound system in natural Microcystis bloom water (initial pilot Chl-a 1,135 mg/m3, 4.89 x 10^6 cells/mL, microcystin 8.8 ug/L). Algal reduction was measured in the supernatant after 1 h of settling, so it counts damaged or sunk cells rather than confirmed kills. The pilot used gentle manual stirring; the distance test used no mixing; the raceway had 5.8 cm/s flow and initial densities varied between runs (222-1,016 mg/m3 Chl-a). Ultrasonication efficiencies were 0.8-15.2 m3/kWh. No untreated controls are described in the text read, and there is no long-term regrowth follow-up.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record's '50-90% in the 4 m3 pond' should be >40% (Chl-a) and >60% (cells) after 10 min in the raceway; the 80-90% figures come from the 100 L pilot within 1 m. Reductions are measured after 1 h settling, and microcystin release increased.

title: Selective Control of Cyanobacteria in Eutrophic Pond by a Combined Device of Ultrasonication and Water Pumps
authors: Ahn C-Y, Joung S-H, Choi A, Kim H-S, Jang K-Y, Oh H-M
scale: 9,000 m3 eutrophic pond vs untreated neighbouring pond
dose: Ultrasonic apparatus plus water pumps to spread sonicated water
result: Chlorophyll-a and total algae in the treated pond were 61% and 53% of the control pond; cyanobacterial growth was selectively inhibited. Cyanobacteria share rose again within days when the device was stopped.
env_effects: Green algae proportion increased; effect not persistent after switch-off; unreplicated pond comparison.

title: In Situ Algal Bloom Control by the Integration of Ultrasonic Radiation and Jet Circulation to Flushing
authors: Nakano K, Lee TJ, Matsumura M
scale: Lake Senba, Mito, Japan (33 ha, 365,000 m3, mean depth 1.0 m); 10 USRS units (12 calculated as needed), each with two 100 W, 200 kHz transducers plus a water-jet circulator
dose: Ultrasonic radiation + jet circulation combined with river-water flushing at a target 75,600 m3/day (residence time 4.8 days)
result: Before the test, chlorophyll-a peaked at 200 ug/L and SS at 100 mg/L with transparency <10 cm; in 1998, with the target flushing volume, SS stayed low and transparency improved, though a chlorophyll-a peak still occurred in June. In 1999 flushing fell below target and chlorophyll-a and SS rose again in summer.
env_effects: Summer COD peaks fell from 30 mg/L to 12 (1998) and 18 mg/L (1999); the summer T-P peak (0.35 mg/L) disappeared, with T-P around 0.1 mg/L; the jet circulator also aerates the bottom.
key_details: Whole-lake before/after trial with no control lake, sampled at three stations. Ultrasound was used only to slow cyanobacterial growth (M. aeruginosa) below the flushing dilution rate of 0.207/day; flushing was the main removal mechanism. Only 10 of the 12 calculated units were installed because of budget, positioned by computer simulation. Correlation analysis before and after the test was used to separate the effects; results depended strongly on inflow volume. Each unit drew about 1.9 kW in total (0.2 kW for sonication).

title: Ultrasonic Treatment of Algae in a New Jersey Reservoir
authors: Schneider OD, Weinrich LA, Brezinski S
scale: Canoe Brook Reservoir 1, Short Hills NJ; 4 ultrasonic buoys
dose: 4 LG Sonic MPC buoys (1 master, 3 slaves); programs changed during the season (Anabaena, then general cyanobacteria on Aug 25, then Aphanizomenon on Sep 9)
duration: May 13 to (mid) November 12, 2014; master buoy lost communication Sep 24
result: Algae stayed <2,000/mL until Aug 13, when opening the Reservoir 2 inlet seeded Aphanizomenon, which the Anabaena and general-cyanobacteria programs did not control (counts >20,000/mL). After the Aphanizomenon-specific program, Sep 17-24 showed ~93% removal by cell counts and ~63% by phycocyanin/chlorophyll fluorescence; counts rose again weeks after the master buoy failed.
env_effects: Not assessed for non-target organisms; geosmin generally lower in Reservoir 1 than Reservoir 2.
key_details: Utility field study at Canoe Brook Reservoir 1 (Short Hills, NJ) with weekly sampling for algal counts (including dynamic particle imaging), TOC, fluorescence EEM, geosmin/MIB and plant operating data. Comparisons were against earlier years (copper-treated before 2012; DAF plant from 2012) and against untreated Reservoir 2, whose cyanobacteria counts were up to an order of magnitude higher through early August. 2014 weather was within the 2008-2013 range but slightly drier. Unreplicated single reservoir; the effect depended on picking the right program for the dominant taxon, and the 93% figure covers one week.
fulltext_discrepancy: The record gives no algal effect size; the full text shows the device failed against Aphanizomenon for several weeks (counts >20,000/mL) until the program was changed, then ~93% cell-count removal over Sep 17-24. Reservoir 2 served as an untreated comparison, so 'no control reservoir' is not quite right.

title: Sound field and water quality in reservoirs using ultrasound as a management strategy to control cyanobacteria blooms
authors: Tischer MA, Murphy KA, Weaver CR, Crafton-Nelson E, Weavers LK
scale: Five Ohio drinking-water reservoirs (3.8 x 10^5 to 5.4 x 10^6 m3) with 1-4 commercial ultrasound units from three manufacturers; at Del-Co, treated reservoir 3 vs untreated reservoirs 2 (upstream) and 4 (downstream)
dose: Commercial units; measured field sound pressures and frequencies
duration: Two field seasons (2022-2023); e.g. five sampling dates at Wilmington in 2022
result: Sound pressure decayed exponentially from each unit, and turbidity, chlorophyll-a, phycocyanin and temperature showed no significant change with distance from the source (least-squares test, p=0.05). Chl-a and phycocyanin fell sequentially from upstream to downstream reservoirs regardless of treatment, which the authors attribute to settling; they conclude ultrasound had no effect.
key_details: Field survey combining hydrophone sound-field mapping (plus anechoic-tank tests of unit directionality) with EXO2 sonde water-quality transects. Maximum transducer pressure was 11 kPa, two orders of magnitude below that needed to collapse gas vesicles, and kHz frequencies are three orders below the MHz needed for resonance; the units operate below the cavitation threshold. Attenuation coefficients varied within a water body by a factor of 2 (low frequency) and 7 (high frequency). Only one location had control reservoirs, and the others were sampled intensively at two sites and once at three.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record's claim that attenuation was '~10x faster than in pure water' was not found in the text read; the paper cites pure water alpha = 0.0022 dB/cm/MHz and reports within-reservoir variation of 2-7x.

title: Effects of ultrasonic algal control devices on fish
authors: Getchell RG, George E, Rice AN, Malatos JM, Chambers BM, Griefen A, Nieder C, Rudstam LG
scale: Oneida Lake nearshore surveys (on/off) plus hydroacoustics; lab: 700 L tanks, 20 fish per tank, device on in 2 of 3 tanks per species trial
dose: One Quattro-DB ultrasonic unit (Hydro BioScience): 468 ms pulses every second, energy 2-250 kHz (to 500 kHz), mean SPL 199.9 dB and max 212.3 dB re 1 uPa; estimated source level 215.5 dB
result: Nearshore fish density (excluding round goby, 88% of observations) was 0.12 fish/m2 with the unit off and 0.13 with it on, with no significant difference. In 14-day tank exposures, no effects were detected on behaviour, feeding or tissues of fish or tadpoles.
env_effects: No detected harm to fish or tadpoles (algal efficacy not measured).
key_details: Non-target safety study, not an algal efficacy test. The authors first measured the device's actual acoustic output with calibrated hydrophones in the field and lab, finding energy well outside the manufacturer's stated bands (down to ~9.8 kHz and up to 500 kHz). Field work at Oneida Lake compared fish communities with the device on and off; lab trials used resident New York species and wild tadpoles (Lithobates spp., American toad), 20 animals per tank, 2 exposed tanks and 1 control per trial. Tank replication per species is small (2 vs 1).
fulltext_discrepancy: One device model (Quattro-DB) was tested, not several devices.
